name: Iraq
card_headline: Iraq's prime minister is pressing Kataib Hezbollah to leave Jurf al-Sakhar after the US exit, and seeks IMF help for an economy set to shrink 16 percent
card_summary: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, a former banker with no prior government experience, took office in May after six months of deadlock. US forces left on 30 September. The US-Israeli war on Iran cut oil exports from 3.36 million barrels a day in February to 131,000 in April, and they recovered to about 3.5 million in October. The IMF projects a 16 percent contraction this year. In November Baghdad gave Kataib Hezbollah a deadline to leave Jurf al-Sakhar, then reached a compromise with it.
card_local: Rudaw quotes a State Department spokesperson saying Washington expects Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable, and Shafaq quotes Lt Gen Saad Maan calling the Jurf al-Sakhar redeployment permanent. [1][2]
card_international: Reuters reports that Baghdad and Kataib Hezbollah reached a compromise on 19 November, with Kataib forces to move to other areas. [3] AFP reports the IMF said on 29 October it is preparing a new programme for Iraq. [4]
card_scholar: Crisis Group (May) calls a gradual, phased approach to disarmament Zaidi's most viable option. [5] Carnegie (September) argues Baghdad should reform the PMF rather than press factions to disarm. [6]
context_md: Iraq held parliamentary elections on 11 November 2025, and the Shia Coordination Framework won about 165 of 329 seats. [7] After months of deadlock parliament approved a partial government under Ali al-Zaidi on 14 May 2026. [5] The US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February 2026 and made Iraq a battleground. [5] Before the war Iraq exported about 3.5 million barrels of oil a day through the Strait of Hormuz, and oil produced about 90 percent of government revenue. [8] The UN mission in Iraq (UNAMI) ended its mandate on 31 December 2025. [7] The US-led coalition ended its mission and US forces left on 30 September 2026, ending a 12-year operation against ISIL. [9][10] The Popular Mobilization Forces, about 230,000 strong, include Iran-aligned factions that have not all accepted state control of their weapons. [7]

sections.title: A partial coalition built by compromise now runs Iraq, six months after the vote
sections.body_md:
Iraq held parliamentary elections on 11 November 2025. The electoral commission reported 56.11 percent turnout, measured against registered biometric cardholders, while the Atlantic Council's Iraq Initiative cites an estimate of roughly 41 percent of Iraqis aged 18 and over. [7][11] The Shia Coordination Framework won about 165 of 329 seats, and Shia parties together about 180. [7] The Sadrist Movement boycotted the vote. [11]

The Framework then stalled for months. Crisis Group says judiciary head Faiq Zaidan brokered the choice of Ali al-Zaidi, a businessman with no prior political or government experience, and that Washington and Tehran both welcomed it. [5] The Atlantic Council adds that the Framework's leading contenders had failed to agree. [11] Parliament elected the PUK's Nizar Amedi president on 11 April 2026, and approved Zaidi's partial government on 14 May. [11][7] The EUAA counts 14 of 23 ministerial nominees confirmed in May. [7]

On 15 October parliament approved 11 further portfolios, including Nayef al-Shammari at defence and Yasir al-Maliki at interior, and three deputy prime ministers. One of them, Laith al-Khazali, is a senior leader of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, which the US designated a foreign terrorist organisation in 2020. [8] A vote on the migration and displacement minister was postponed. [8] Crisis Group reports that US pressure kept parties linked to designated terrorist organisations out of the cabinet, and that the US sanctioned Maliki's oil nominee days before the May vote. [5]

lenses.local: Rudaw quotes a State Department spokesperson saying Washington expects Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, with AP and Reuters, reports the October cabinet vote together with warnings of severe liquidity shortages. [8]
lenses.scholar: The Atlantic Council describes a compromise pick chosen after the Framework's leading contenders failed to agree. [11]

sections.title: Jurf al-Sakhar is the test: Baghdad gave Kataib Hezbollah a deadline, then a compromise followed
sections.body_md:
Zaidi has made bringing weapons under state control a stated priority. [8] The original deadline of 30 September 2026 for armed groups to integrate or disarm has been pushed to 30 June 2027. [7][9] The EUAA puts the Popular Mobilization Forces at about 230,000 personnel in 60 to 70 brigades, with a core controlled by Iran-aligned factions: Badr, Kataib Hezbollah (up to about 10,000 fighters), Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada. [7] Saraya al-Salam, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib al-Imam Ali have moved toward integration or announced they would leave the PMF, though by late July neither of the last two had laid down arms. [6][7] Kataib Hezbollah, Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada refused to disarm until US troops left. [7]

The sharpest test is Jurf al-Sakhar, an area of roughly 345 square kilometres about 60 km southwest of Baghdad that Kataib Hezbollah has held since the PMF retook it from ISIL, which had seized it in 2014, and later sealed it to state institutions. [12] On 16 November Reuters reported, citing Iraqi officials, that the group ran a network that tapped a 26-inch crude pipeline carrying at least 200,000 barrels a day, drew oil into pits, loaded tankers from hidden pumps and ran a small secret refinery, earning hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. [13] Two oil officials said it was too early to quantify the losses. [13] Zaidi dismissed nine senior security and oil officials and referred suspects to court. [13] Kataib Hezbollah denies the smuggling and calls the campaign an effort to seize its weapons. [13] Al Jazeera reports the group mobilised about 8,000 fighters toward the area, while one MP told Rudaw it had more than 40,000 there, a figure no other source in this draft confirms. [12][1]

On 19 November three senior security officials told Reuters that Baghdad and Kataib Hezbollah had reached a compromise brokered by senior Shia leaders, under which Kataib forces would move to other areas. Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani had arrived in Baghdad to help defuse the tension. [3] Shafaq quotes Lt Gen Saad Maan calling the redeployment permanent, with the army, Federal Police, PMF and Energy Police dividing security duties under a new command headquarters. [2][14] Whether the Friday 20 November deadline passed with a completed handover is not confirmed in the sources read for this page.

lenses.local: Kurdistan24 and Shafaq report Zaidi's order to move more forces to Jurf al-Sakhar and the redeployment plan, and Rudaw reports that the Framework agreed to replace Kataib Hezbollah there with another PMF formation. [15][2][1]
lenses.international: Reuters and AFP carry the smuggling allegations, Qaani's arrival and the compromise. [13][3][14]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House says formal integration does not necessarily transfer loyalty or control, and that the test is whether factions give up drones and rockets. [16] Carnegie's Ali Al-Mawlawi argues for reforming the PMF rather than pressing factions to disarm. [6]

sections.title: The US has left, but the Iran war still runs through Iraq
sections.body_md:
The US-led coalition's mission ended on 30 September 2026, and US forces left their remaining bases as the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIL expired. [9] The Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell described an orderly departure from Erbil Air Base, and CENTCOM said the coalition task force moved its headquarters to Jordan. [10] The EUAA dates the coalition's announcement of its exit from federal Iraq to 18 January, and says US forces left Ain al-Asad on 17 January. [7] Iraq took control of the US headquarters at Baghdad airport on 28 September, and Lt Gen Saad Maan said the handover does not end security cooperation. [9]

The US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February 2026. [9] The Kurdistan Region's Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs says the region has faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks since then. [9] The EUAA puts the number at almost 500 strikes by Iran and aligned Iraqi militias between 28 February and 8 April, citing Crisis Group, and says a ceasefire was announced on 8 April. [7] Carnegie says the ceasefire later broke down and hostilities resumed in early July. [6] On 29 July Saudi Arabia and US Central Command struck Iran-backed militias in Iraq after Riyadh said drones launched from Iraq had targeted its oil facilities. The PMF said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 wounded, and the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied any role. Iraq's presidency denounced the strikes. [17] On 12 November Al Jazeera described no formal ceasefire, stalled talks and full-scale fighting on hold. [18]

Whether US personnel remain is reported thinly. Shafaq quoted the politician Bahaa al-Araji on 20 September saying US forces would stay to protect the embassy and diplomatic missions, with no numbers given; no second source was found. [19] On ISIL, Al Jazeera reports the latest UN Secretary-General report calls the group "at its weakest", while Iraqi officials told Reuters it had planned attacks to coincide with the withdrawal. [9] The EUAA notes the UN estimate of about 3,000 fighters across Iraq and Syria, most of them in Syria, and says attacks in Iraq in 2025 were at an all-time low. [7]

lenses.local: Shafaq's single-sourced report says US forces would stay for embassy protection after the coalition exit. [19]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera with AP and Reuters, and AP via ABC, report the 30 September completion and the Kurdish officials' concern about air defence. [9][10]
lenses.scholar: Hassan Barari of the University of Jordan told Al Jazeera it is unlikely Iraq can currently protect its airspace from missiles and drones, and Crisis Group's Ali Vaez calls the US-Iran equilibrium inherently unstable. [9][18]

sections.title: Oil is 90 percent of state revenue, and the Hormuz closure took exports to 131,000 barrels a day
sections.body_md:
Iraq's oil exports fell from 3.36 million barrels a day in February to 131,000 in April after the Iran war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. [20] Monthly oil revenue had been about $7 billion. [20] Exports recovered to about 3.5 million barrels a day in October from 2.65 million in September, according to Iraqi energy officials cited by Reuters. [21] On 8 November Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Iraq had reached understandings with the US to let exports pass through a lane near Oman, and put Iraq's losses from the war and export disruption at $60 billion. [21] Shipping stays erratic: Al Jazeera, citing Kpler, reports five commodity vessels crossed on 7 November and none on 8 November. [18] On 17 November Iraq resumed pumping crude through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey at 120,000 barrels a day, with the oil minister saying flows would rise toward 500,000. Baghdad has also begun work on a Basra-Haditha pipeline with a stated capacity of 2.5 million barrels a day. [20]

The state absorbed the shock through reserves, debt and the currency. The National reports foreign reserves fell from about $109 billion to $80.6 billion, that Iraq has formally requested an IMF programme, its first since 2016, and that the IMF projects a 16 percent contraction in 2026. [22] AFP reports the IMF said on 29 October that it is engaging Iraq as it prepares a new programme. [4] The central bank moved the official rate from 1,300 to 1,500 dinars to the dollar in October, which Iraq Business News calls a 13.3 percent devaluation and Al Jazeera puts at almost 15 percent. [23][8] Zaidi said his government inherited public debt above 208 trillion dinars and that the state needs about 10 trillion dinars a month for salaries and critical spending. [8]

The draft 2027 budget sets spending near 217.2 trillion dinars, revenue at 174.2 trillion and a deficit of about 43 trillion, built on $58 a barrel and exports of around 4 million barrels a day including Kurdistan. [22] Shafaq reported in September that a deficit above 60 trillion dinars was possible. [24] Zaidi directed that 500,000 contract and daily-wage workers be made permanent. [22] Baghdad economist Nabil Al Marsoomi called the budget populist. [22]

lenses.local: Shafaq reported in September that the 2027 deficit could exceed 60 trillion dinars and that the payroll must absorb new appointments and permanent hiring. [24]
lenses.international: Reuters, AFP and The National report the export collapse and recovery, the IMF request and the budget draft. [21][4][20][22]

sections.title: The Kurdistan Region has no new cabinet two years after its vote, and its pay still depends on Baghdad
sections.body_md:
The Kurdistan Region voted on 20 October 2024 and still has no new government. The KDP won 39 seats and the PUK 23, and the two remain deadlocked over how to share power and over administrative, security and financial powers. [25] Masrour Barzani's cabinet stays in office, and Barzani has said steps toward forming a government have been delayed too long. [25] The EUAA says the KDP and PUK are effectively administering separate areas. [7] On 4 November 52 lawmakers attended a session that reactivated the sixth parliamentary term and elected Vala Farid of the KDP speaker. [26] On 18 November the Federal Supreme Court dismissed a case against that continuation, saying it lacks jurisdiction, and the court's ruling is not a decision on constitutionality. [26]

Pay is the pressure point. A Middle East Online report, undated and without a byline, says Baghdad ties salary transfers to oil and non-oil revenue handovers and calls the money temporary advances, while Erbil calls salaries a red line. It says the Region was allocated 58.3 trillion dinars under the 2023 to 2025 budget framework and received 24.3 trillion, about 41 percent, and that shortfalls continued into 2026. [27] These figures are that outlet's own and were not checked against budget documents. The draft 2027 budget keeps the Region's share at 12.7 percent of actual spending, while Shafaq cited 14.1 percent based on the latest census in September. [22][24] Masrour Barzani said no final agreement had been reached with Baghdad. [22]

Security is the second pressure. Kurdish officials say US air defences in Erbil helped intercept Iranian missiles and drones, and the Peshmerga ministry called the lack of a replacement system deeply concerning. [9][10] A drone attack on Barzani's office in August was, according to officials, launched from Iranian territory. [9] The EUAA reports about 5,000 Turkish troops at roughly 50 bases in Erbil, Ninewa and Dohuk, and says thousands of villagers cannot return because Turkish forces turned villages into bases. [7]

lenses.local: Shafaq and Kurdistan24 report the cabinet deadlock, the reactivated parliament and the court's jurisdiction ruling. [25][26]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and AP report Kurdish officials' alarm over the loss of US air defences. [9][10]
lenses.scholar: The EUAA describes separate KDP and PUK administrations and the Turkish military presence. [7]

sections.title: Mass trials of 5,700 ISIS suspects, a full death row and a press ranked 162nd
sections.body_md:
Between 21 January and 12 February 2026 CENTCOM transferred more than 5,700 male former ISIL members from Syrian detention into Iraqi custody. [7] Human Rights Watch says they hold citizenship of 42 countries, are held in Nasiriyah and Karkh prisons, and face risks of enforced disappearance, unfair trials and torture, and that the transfers appear to violate non-refoulement. [28] Iraq's government called the move a preemptive step against prison breaks, and the Supreme Judicial Council said on 8 February that the suspects would be prosecuted under Iraqi law. [28] Amnesty counts 5,704 detainees from 67 countries, at least 157 of them under 18, and says trials began on 20 September under the 1969 Penal Code and the 2005 Anti-Terrorism Law, with Iraqi courts repeatedly relying on confessions extracted through torture. [29] The two groups' country counts differ and were not reconciled. HRW says about 8,000 prisoners are on death row and that Iraq executed six people on 10 February. [28] Amnesty says executions slowed after a 2025 amnesty law and resumed in early 2026. [29]

The press is under pressure from several directions. RSF ranks Iraq 162nd of 180 in its 2026 index with a score of 28.85, down from 155th, counts three journalists detained, and says killings of journalists rarely lead to investigations. [30] The US freelance journalist Shelly Kittleson was seized in Baghdad on 31 March and freed on 7 April. Kataib Hezbollah said it released her on the condition that she leave the country, and two officials told AP that Iraq agreed to release detained militia members in exchange. [31] The Journalists' Rights Defense Association counted 182 violations in 2025, including two killings, and Metro Center counted 315 in the Kurdistan Region, nearly double the previous year. [32]

HRW's World Report says parliament passed the Ja'afari Personal Status Code on 27 August 2025 without debate, and that a domestic violence law has stalled for over a decade. [33]

lenses.local: Shafaq reports press-freedom violation counts from Iraqi monitors, including 315 in the Kurdistan Region in 2025. [32]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, with AFP and AP, reports Kittleson's abduction and release and the reported prisoner swap. [31]
lenses.scholar: HRW and Amnesty are the main documentary sources on the detainee transfers and trials, and both note the government's stated reasons. [28][29]

sections.title: Water storage recovered this year, while about a million people stay displaced
sections.body_md:
The UN Water Task Force reported on 5 June that live water storage rose from about 3.5 billion to about 20 billion cubic metres after above-normal winter rain, the largest recovery in recent years. [34] That is still below 20 percent of total capacity, and Iraq has lost about 56 billion cubic metres of storage since 2020. [34] The Mosul Dam rose from 280 million cubic metres at the start of 2026 to near full safe operating capacity, while Haditha Dam on the Euphrates stays low because inflow from Turkey has been insufficient. [34] The brief warns that approved summer rice cultivation could erase the gains before the next rainy season. [34] A year earlier the position was worse: in September 2025 Shafaq reported storage below 8 billion cubic metres, reservoirs at 8 percent of capacity and Turkish discharges averaging about 200 cubic metres per second. [35]

Displacement moves more slowly. IOM and UNHCR count 1,031,475 people still displaced, a national figure carried over from December 2024 because funding for new data collection was lacking, and 101,886 people in 20 camps in the Kurdistan Region. [36] NRC gives the same figures and says 295,602 displaced people live in difficult conditions, most displaced for over seven years. [37] IOM and UNHCR list insecurity, missing housing and services, and unclear support after funding cuts as the obstacles to return. [36] Al Jazeera reports that roughly 140,000 displaced residents of Jurf al-Sakhar have effectively been prevented from returning. [12] The EUAA notes that UNAMI's mandate ended on 31 December 2025, which limited casualty recording. [7]

lenses.local: Shafaq's September 2025 report gives the pre-rain baseline of reservoirs at 8 percent of capacity. [35]
lenses.international: NRC and IOM-UNHCR both put the displaced population at about 1.03 million. [37][36]
lenses.scholar: The UN Water Task Force brief is the main technical source on storage recovery and warns that rice planting could erase it. [34]

timeline.text: The Kurdistan Region votes in parliamentary elections and still has no new government two years later.
Iraq holds national parliamentary elections; the commission reports 56.11 percent turnout.
The UN mission in Iraq (UNAMI) mandate ends.
The coalition announces its withdrawal from federal Iraq.
CENTCOM begins transferring ISIS suspects from Syrian detention to Iraq, about 5,700 by 12 February.
The US-Israeli war on Iran begins; Iraq becomes a battleground.
US journalist Shelly Kittleson is seized in Baghdad; she is freed on 7 April.
A ceasefire in the Iran war is announced; oil exports bottom out at 131,000 barrels a day in April.
Parliament approves a partial government led by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
Saudi Arabia and the US strike Iran-backed militias in Iraq; the PMF reports at least 20 killed.
US forces complete their withdrawal and the coalition mission ends.
Parliament approves 11 further cabinet portfolios and three deputy prime ministers.
The IMF says it is preparing a new programme for Iraq.
A government committee enters Jurf al-Sakhar with military backing; nine officials are dismissed.
Iraq resumes pumping crude to Turkey through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline at 120,000 barrels a day.
The Federal Supreme Court dismisses a case against the Kurdistan parliament's continued sixth term.
Baghdad and Kataib Hezbollah reach a compromise over Jurf al-Sakhar; the government's Friday deadline falls on 20 November.

reporters.name: Ahmed Rasheed
reporters.bio: Bylined the Reuters reports of 8, 16 and 19 November 2026 on Iraq's Hormuz export understandings, Kataib Hezbollah oil smuggling and the Jurf al-Sakhar compromise.
reporters.why: His filings carry most of the English-language wire reporting on Baghdad's militia and oil stories this month.
reporters.label: Reuters via Al-Monitor

reporters.name: Diyar Kurda
reporters.bio: Bylined the 18 November 2026 Rudaw report quoting a State Department spokesperson and Iraqi MPs on the Jurf al-Sakhr standoff.
reporters.why: Gives Kurdish-region and parliamentary voices on the militia crisis that wire copy often omits.
reporters.label: Rudaw

reporters.name: Sangar Akrayi
reporters.bio: Bylined the 16 November 2026 Kurdistan24 report relaying Reuters on the tapped pipeline at Jurf al-Sakhr.
reporters.why: Shows how the Kurdistan Region's English-language press relays and frames the Baghdad militia story.
reporters.label: Kurdistan24

reporters.name: Dler Mohammed
reporters.bio: Bylined the 18 November 2026 report on the Federal Supreme Court's dismissal of the case against the Kurdistan parliament's sixth term.
reporters.why: Tracks the legal side of the Erbil-Baghdad dispute through case numbers and court language.
reporters.label: Kurdistan24

reporters.name: Sinan Mahmoud
reporters.bio: Bylined the 26 October 2026 report on Iraq's draft 2027 budget, datelined Baghdad.
reporters.why: Sets out the budget figures and quotes a Baghdad economist and the Kurdistan prime minister in one place.
reporters.label: The National

reporters.name: Mohammad Mansour
reporters.bio: Bylined the 18 November 2026 Al Jazeera explainer on Jurf al-Sakhar and the government's push to control it.
reporters.why: Gives the area's history and the displaced residents' position, which other reports skip.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Lahib Higel
reporters.role: Interim Deputy Program Director, Middle East and North Africa, International Crisis Group
reporters.bio: Author of Crisis Group's 28 May 2026 analysis of Iraq's new government, and guest on a War on the Rocks podcast on 22 August 2026.
reporters.why: Her analysis argues a gradual, phased approach to disarmament is Zaidi's most viable option.
reporters.label: International Crisis Group via ecoi.net

reporters.name: Ali Al-Mawlawi
reporters.bio: Author of the 18 September 2026 Carnegie Diwan piece on PMF reform and disarmament; the page describes the firm as focused on Iraq.
reporters.why: Names which factions have integrated and which have not, and proposes specific changes to the stalled PMF bill.
reporters.label: Carnegie Endowment

reporters.name: Renad Mansour
reporters.role: Deputy director, MENA Programme, and director, Iraq Initiative, Chatham House
reporters.bio: Guest on the Middle East Institute's Middle East Focus podcast, recorded 9 June 2026, on Iraq's new government.
reporters.why: Covers the war's effect on Iran-linked militia networks, attacks on the Kurdistan Region and shifting ties with Tehran and Washington.
reporters.label: Middle East Institute podcast

reporters.name: Sarah Sanbar
reporters.bio: Quoted in HRW's 17 February 2026 release on the ISIS detainees transferred from Syria.
reporters.why: HRW's Iraq researcher on fair trials for the detainees and for victims of ISIS crimes.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

books.title: The Shi'is of Iraq
books.author: Yitzhak Nakash
books.why: Kanan Makiya recommends it on Five Books as an account of how modern Iraqi Shia took shape through the settlement of nomadic tribes in the 19th century.
books.label: Princeton University Press

books.title: Iraq Since 1958: From Revolution to Dictatorship
books.author: Marion Farouk-Sluglett and Peter Sluglett
books.why: A political history after the fall of the monarchy, tracing the army's role in successive coups and the Ba'ath regime, per Five Books. The year is that of the revised paperback edition.
books.label: Blackwell's (I. B. Tauris edition)

books.title: The Forever War
books.author: Dexter Filkins
books.why: A New York Times reporter's first-hand account of Iraq after 2003, which Makiya recommends on Five Books for its picture of the civil wars that followed the invasion.
books.label: Kirkus Reviews

podcasts.title: Attacked by All Sides: Iraq's New Government Faces Old Problems
podcasts.why: Covers Zaidi's first weeks, the economy, armed factions and attacks on the Kurdistan Region.

podcasts.title: The Tricky Problem of Disarming and Integrating Pro-Iran Militias in Iraq
podcasts.why: Set before the 30 September deadline; the militias' ties to the government and the difficulty of folding them into the security forces.

podcasts.title: Why Iraq is the most fragile front in the US-Israel war on Iran
podcasts.why: An early-war look at strikes on Iran-backed groups, militia responses and disrupted oil flows. Al Jazeera is state-funded by Qatar.

media.creator: Zaradasht Ahmed (Al Jazeera Witness)
media.why: Follows three men restoring cultural life in Mosul after the fight to retake it from ISIL. Al Jazeera is state-funded by Qatar.

factchecks.claim: All US forces have left Iraq.
factchecks.by: Wire and television headlines on 30 September 2026, and President Trump's remarks the same day
factchecks.evidence: The US-led coalition mission ended on 30 September, and AP-based copy says the military completed its withdrawal. Shafaq reported on 20 September, citing one Iraqi politician, that US forces would remain to protect the embassy and diplomatic missions, and CENTCOM described a shift to a bilateral defence relationship. No troop numbers were found, so the size of any remaining presence is unknown.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters filed three Iraq reports between 8 and 20 November that this draft read, and AFP and AP supply further wire copy [21][13][3][4][10]. Crisis Group, Carnegie, Chatham House and the Atlantic Council publish regularly on Iraq [5][6][16][11]. Attention follows the Iran war and the militias, while water, displacement and the detainee trials surface mostly through NGO and local reports [37][29][32].

severity.basis: The Kurdistan Region's Peshmerga ministry counts more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks since 28 February, the PMF says US and Saudi strikes killed at least 20 of its members on 29 July, and Kataib Hezbollah stood off against the state at Jurf al-Sakhar [9][17][3]. The EUAA says ISIL attacks in 2025 were at an all-time low [7].

About 1.03 million people remain displaced and 101,886 live in Kurdistan Region camps [36]. UN reporting shows water storage recovering this year, and the sources read report no famine or epidemic [34].
Iraq is trying 5,704 transferred ISIS suspects amid Amnesty's findings on torture-based confessions, about 8,000 prisoners are on death row, and RSF ranks Iraq 162nd of 180 [29][28][30].

Exports fell to 131,000 barrels a day in April, reserves dropped from about $109 billion to $80.6 billion, the IMF projects a 16 percent contraction and Iraq has asked for a programme [20][22]. The dinar was devalued in October [23].

Exports recovered to about 3.5 million barrels a day and a government formed after months of deadlock [21][5], but there is no formal US-Iran ceasefire and the militia disarmament deadline moved to June 2027 [18][7].

parts.basis: The US ended its coalition mission on 30 September but keeps a bilateral security relationship and sanctions, Saudi Arabia joined US strikes in Iraq on 29 July, Iran's Quds Force commander went to Baghdad to defuse the Jurf al-Sakhar crisis, and Turkey keeps about 5,000 troops at roughly 50 bases [9][5][17][3][7].
Before the war Iraq exported about 3.5 million barrels a day through the Strait of Hormuz, which generated 90 percent of government revenue, and exports were 3.36 million in February [8][20].

Iran-aligned groups launched attacks from Iraqi territory despite Baghdad's neutrality policy, Saudi Arabia says drones aimed at its oil facilities came from Iraq (the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denies it), and the Kurdistan Region took more than 1,000 strikes [5][17][9].
Iraq holds 5,704 transferred detainees from 67 countries, and about 1.03 million people are displaced inside the country [29][36].
HRW says the transfers of detainees from Syria appear to violate non-refoulement, and the PMF and Iraq's presidency called the US-Saudi strikes a violation of sovereignty [28][17].

summary: Iraq matters beyond its borders through the oil that leaves via Hormuz, its role as an arena for the US-Iran confrontation, and armed groups that operate from its territory [8][17][5]. Its human reach scores lower because the sources read give few cross-border population figures beyond the detainees [29][36].
gi.up: A return to full-scale US-Iran fighting, a clash between the army and Kataib Hezbollah, or a renewed Hormuz closure.
gi.down: A signed US-Iran settlement that keeps Hormuz open and completed integration or disarmament of the armed factions.

gaps: Arabic-language Iraqi outlets and the state Iraqi News Agency were not read directly; local sourcing here is English-language editions of Rudaw, Kurdistan24 and Shafaq, and Iraq has few independent local outlets in English.
The political affiliation of Rudaw and Kurdistan24 was not checked in this session; treat Kurdistan Region coverage as possibly party-aligned.
The outcome of the 20 November deadline at Jurf al-Sakhar is not confirmed; the latest sources are dated 19 and 20 November.
The 16 November oil-smuggling allegations come from unnamed Iraqi officials via Reuters, and Kataib Hezbollah denies them. The 40,000-fighter figure rests on one MP quoted by Rudaw.

Accounts of the Iran war ceasefire differ: the EUAA gives 8 April, Carnegie says it broke down in early July, and Al Jazeera on 12 November describes no formal ceasefire. The US-Iran negotiating record was not read directly.
The size and role of any remaining US presence rests on one Shafaq report citing one politician; no troop numbers were found.
Civilian casualty totals for 2026 were not found; UNAMI's mandate ended in December 2025 and the EUAA excerpt read did not include national incident counts.
The national displacement total of 1,031,475 is a December 2024 figure. HRW counts the transferred detainees' nationalities at 42 and Amnesty at 67; these were not reconciled.

Kurdistan salary figures come from an undated, unbylined Middle East Online article and were not checked against budget documents. The Region's share of the 2027 draft differs between sources (12.7 and 14.1 percent).

The budget, deficit and IMF figures are drafts or forecasts from secondary reporting; IMF and World Bank primary documents for 2026 were not opened. Cabinet confirmation counts (14 of 23 nominees in May, 11 portfolios in October) were not reconciled.
The EUAA report was read through its first 100,000 of 463,579 characters; ACLED data were not opened directly.
No peer-reviewed or book-length scholarship on events after 2025 was reviewed; the three books listed are older background works, with years taken from catalogue or review pages.
The water-recovery figures come from a single UN brief, and the September 2025 comparison from one Shafaq article with inconsistent units.

local_md:
Rudaw quotes a State Department spokesperson saying Washington expects Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable. [1]

Kurdistan24 and Shafaq report Zaidi's order to move more forces to Jurf al-Sakhar and the redeployment plan, and Rudaw reports that the Framework agreed to replace Kataib Hezbollah there with another PMF formation. [15][2][1]

Shafaq's single-sourced report says US forces would stay for embassy protection after the coalition exit. [19]

Shafaq reported in September that the 2027 deficit could exceed 60 trillion dinars and that the payroll must absorb new appointments and permanent hiring. [24]

Shafaq and Kurdistan24 report the cabinet deadlock, the reactivated parliament and the court's jurisdiction ruling. [25][26]

Shafaq reports press-freedom violation counts from Iraqi monitors, including 315 in the Kurdistan Region in 2025. [32]

Shafaq's September 2025 report gives the pre-rain baseline of reservoirs at 8 percent of capacity. [35]
international_md:
Al Jazeera, with AP and Reuters, reports the October cabinet vote together with warnings of severe liquidity shortages. [8]

Reuters and AFP carry the smuggling allegations, Qaani's arrival and the compromise. [13][3][14]

Al Jazeera with AP and Reuters, and AP via ABC, report the 30 September completion and the Kurdish officials' concern about air defence. [9][10]

Reuters, AFP and The National report the export collapse and recovery, the IMF request and the budget draft. [21][4][20][22]

Al Jazeera and AP report Kurdish officials' alarm over the loss of US air defences. [9][10]

Al Jazeera, with AFP and AP, reports Kittleson's abduction and release and the reported prisoner swap. [31]

NRC and IOM-UNHCR both put the displaced population at about 1.03 million. [37][36]
scholar_md:
The Atlantic Council describes a compromise pick chosen after the Framework's leading contenders failed to agree. [11]

Chatham House says formal integration does not necessarily transfer loyalty or control, and that the test is whether factions give up drones and rockets. [16] Carnegie's Ali Al-Mawlawi argues for reforming the PMF rather than pressing factions to disarm. [6]

Hassan Barari of the University of Jordan told Al Jazeera it is unlikely Iraq can currently protect its airspace from missiles and drones, and Crisis Group's Ali Vaez calls the US-Iran equilibrium inherently unstable. [9][18]

The EUAA describes separate KDP and PUK administrations and the Turkish military presence. [7]

HRW and Amnesty are the main documentary sources on the detainee transfers and trials, and both note the government's stated reasons. [28][29]

The UN Water Task Force brief is the main technical source on storage recovery and warns that rice planting could erase it. [34]
